'''''Valemax''''' ships are a fleet of [[very large ore carrier]]s (VLOC) owned or chartered by the [[Brazil]]ian mining company [[Vale (mining company)|Vale S.A.]] to carry [[iron ore]] from Brazil to European and Asian ports. With a capacity ranging from 380,000 to 400,000 tons [[deadweight tonnage|deadweight]], the vessels meet the [[Chinamax]] standard of ship measurements for limits on [[Draft (hull)|draft]] and [[Beam (nautical)|beam]]. ''Valemax'' ships are the largest [[bulk carrier]]s ever constructed, when measuring deadweight tonnage or [[length overall]], and are amongst the [[list of world's longest ships|longest ships]] of any type currently in service.<ref name="dnv1">[http://www.dnv.com/industry/maritime/publicationsanddownloads/publications/updates/bulk/2011/2_2011/DSMEdeliveringValeBrasiltheworldslargestorecarrier.asp DSME delivering Vale Brasil, the world's largest ore carrier] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927133050/http://www.dnv.com/industry/maritime/publicationsanddownloads/publications/updates/bulk/2011/2_2011/DSMEdeliveringValeBrasiltheworldslargestorecarrier.asp |date=27 September 2011 }}. Det Norske Veritas, 1 June 2011. Retrieved 1 September 2011</ref>

The first ''Valemax'' vessel, [[MS Ore Brasil|''Vale Brasil'']], was delivered in 2011. Initially, all 35 ships of the first series were expected to be in service by 2013, but the last ship was not delivered until September 2016. In late 2015 and early 2016, Chinese shipping companies ordered 30 more ships with deliveries in 2018–2020. Three additional vessels were ordered by a Japanese shipping company, bringing the total number of ''Valemax'' vessels to 68 {{asof|2020|lc=y}}.

== Construction ==

=== First series ===

In 2008, Vale placed orders for twelve 400,000-ton ''Valemax'' ships to be constructed by Jiangsu Rongsheng Heavy Industries (RSHI) in [[China]] and ordered seven more ships from [[South Korea]]n [[Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering]] (DSME) in 2009. In addition sixteen more ships of similar size were ordered from Chinese and South Korean shipyards for other shipping companies, and [[Chartering (shipping)|chartered]] to Vale under long-term contracts. The first vessel was delivered in 2011 and the last in 2016.<ref name="equasis_seapontadamadeira">{{csr|register=E|id=9575503|shipname=Sea Ponta da Madeira|access-date=27 October 2016}}</ref>

==== Jiangsu Rongsheng Heavy Industries ====

[[File:Vale Dalian shipyard 20111226.jpg|thumb|left|400px|The 400,000-ton ''Vale Dalian'' photographed together with 75,750-ton ''Guo Yan 20'', showing the size difference between a ''Valemax'' vessel and a [[Panamax]] bulk carrier. Note unladen hulls riding high in the water.]]

The first ''Valemax'' vessels were ordered on 3 August 2008 when Vale signed a contract with the Chinese shipbuilder Jiangsu Rongsheng Heavy Industries (RSHI) for the construction of twelve 400,000-ton ore carriers. The development had reportedly started in 2007.<ref name="caixin">[http://english.caixin.com/2012-06-07/100398326.html China Set to Deliver Two Mega-ships to Vale]. ''Caixin'', 6 July 2012. {{retrieved |access-date=18 July 2012}}</ref> The contract, worth $1.6 billion, was the world's biggest single shipbuilding contract by deadweight tonnage.<ref name="dnv3">[http://www.dnv.com/industry/maritime/publicationsanddownloads/publications/updates/bulk/2008/2_2008/BreakingNewsDNVawardedclassfortheworldsbiggestshipbuildingcontractever.asp Breaking News: DNV awarded class for the world's biggest shipbuilding contract ever!] {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20130122051555/http://www.dnv.com/industry/maritime/publicationsanddownloads/publications/updates/bulk/2008/2_2008/BreakingNewsDNVawardedclassfortheworldsbiggestshipbuildingcontractever.asp |date=22 January 2013 }}, Det Norske Veritas, 9 September 2008. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref><ref name="shipbuildingtribune">[http://shipbuildingtribune.com/2011/07/11/china-rshi-launches-worlds-most-advanced-vloc-for-iron-ore-supplier-vale/ China: RSHI Launches World's Most Advanced VLOC for Iron Ore Supplier Vale] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120331190644/http://shipbuildingtribune.com/2011/07/11/china-rshi-launches-worlds-most-advanced-vloc-for-iron-ore-supplier-vale/ |date=31 March 2012 }}. Shipbuilding Tribune, 11 July 2011. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref>

The first Chinese-built ''Valemax'' vessel, [[MS Vale China|''Vale China'']], was launched at the [[Nantong]] shipyard on 9 July 2011 and delivered on 25 November 2011.<ref name="dnv_orechina">{{csr|register=DNV|id=30059|shipname=Ore China|access-date=27 May 2014}}</ref><ref name="4traders">[http://www.4-traders.com/CHINA-RONGSHENG-6888083/news/CHIA-RONG-China-Rongsheng-Hodeavy-Industries-400-000-DWT-Vloc-Named-and-Launched-Lowers-Cost-for-Vale--13701469/ CHIA RONG : China Rongsheng Heavy Industries' 400,000 DWT Vloc Named and Launched – Lowers Cost for Vale and Forges Long-Term Cooperation, First Vlocs to be Delivered Soon]. 4-traders.com, 10 July 2011. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref> Although it was expected that the first Chinese-built ''Valemax'' vessel would call a Chinese port on its maiden voyage,<ref name="reuters2">[https://www.reuters.com/article/vale-china-ship/vale-gets-1st-china-built-mega-iron-ore-carrier-market-shudders-idINL3E7IC0LA20110712 Vale gets 1st China-built mega iron ore carrier, market shudders]. Reuters, 12 July 2011. Retrieved 14 November 2022</ref> the ship was diverted to the new transshipment hub Vale had constructed in Philippines.<ref name="valechina_philippines">[http://www.miningweekly.com/article/with-china-shut-vale-iron-ore-ships-head-to-philippines-2012-01-26 With China shut, Vale iron-ore ships head to Philippines]. Mining Weekly, 26 January 2012. Retrieved 4 February 2012</ref>

The second RSHI-built ''Valemax'' ship for Vale ([[MS Ore Dongjiakou|''Vale Dongjiakou'']]) was delivered on 9 April 2012,<ref name="dnv_oredongjiakou" /> the third ([[MS Vale Dalian|''Vale Dalian'']]) on 20 May,<ref name="dnv_oredalian" /> the fourth ([[MS Ore Hebei|''Vale Hebei'']]) on 28 September,<ref name="dnv_orehebei" /> the fifth ([[MS Ore Shandong|''Vale Shandong'']]) on 7 December 2012,<ref name="dnv_oreshandong" /> the sixth ([[MS Ore Jiangsu|''Vale Jiangsu'']]) on 23 March 2013,<ref name="dnv_yuanzhenhai" /> the seventh ([[MS Yuan Shi Hai|''Vale Caofeidian'']]) on 22 July 2013,<ref name="dnv_yuanshihai" /> the eighth ([[MS Yuan Jian Hai|''Vale Lianyungang'']]) on 22 November 2013,<ref name="dnv_yuanjianhai" /> the ninth ([[MS Ore Majishan|''Ore Majishan'']]; renamed before delivery) on 11 July 2014,<ref name="dnv_yuanzhuohai" /> the tenth ([[MS Ore Tianjin|''Ore Tianjin'']]; renamed before delivery) on 18 October 2014,<ref name="dnv_oretianjin" /> and the eleventh ([[MS Ore Rizhao|''Ore Rizhao'']]; renamed before delivery) on 15 December 2014.<ref name="dnv_orerizhao" /> The twelfth and last ''Valemax'' vessel of the original order by Vale, [[MS Ore Ningbo|''Ore Ningbo'']] (renamed before delivery), was delivered on 23 January 2015.<ref name="dnv_oreningbo" />

On 2 November 2008, [[Oman Shipping Company]] signed a framework agreement with RSHI for the construction of four 400,000-ton vessels to transport iron ore from Brazil to the [[SOHAR Port and Freezone|Port of Sohar]] in [[Oman]], where Vale is expected to open a steel plant in near future.<ref name="omanshipco">[http://www.omanship.co.om/NewsPress%20Releases.html Sultanate and Brazil, Agreement to Lease four ships for Steel Ore] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110424235942/http://www.omanship.co.om/NewsPress%20Releases.html |date=24 April 2011 }}. Oman Shipping Company News Press Releases, 2 November 2008. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref> The shipbuilding contract, worth US$483 million, was signed in July 2009.<ref>[http://store.businessmonitor.com/article/273721 Jiangsu Rongsheng Signs US$483 Newbuild VLOC Deal With Oman Shipping] {{Webarchive|url=https://archive.today/20120719034534/http://store.businessmonitor.com/article/273721 |date=19 July 2012 }}. Business Monitor International, 13 July 2009. Retrieved 4 February 2012</ref> Initially the ships were to be named ''Jazer'', ''Yanqul'', ''Al Kamil'' and ''Wafi'',<ref name="omanshipfleet">[http://www.omanship.co.om/Pages.aspx?P=Fleet Fleet] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111118164252/http://www.omanship.co.om/Pages.aspx?P=Fleet |date=18 November 2011 }}. Oman Shipping Company. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref> but instead they will be named [[MS Liwa Max|''Vale Liwa'']], [[MS Sohar Max|''Vale Sohar'']], [[MS Shinas Max|''Vale Shinas'']] and [[MS Saham Max|''Vale Saham'']]. The steel cutting ceremony for the first two vessels was held on 8 July 2010 and they were launched on 19 March 2012.<ref>[http://www.rshi.cn/en/centerView-267.html RSHI's 400,000 DWT VLOC Began Construction]{{Dead link|date=October 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}. Jiangsu Rongsheng Heavy Industries, 8 July 2010. Retrieved 4 February 2012</ref><ref name="omanlaunch">{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20121017141219/http://worldmaritimenews.com/archives/51555 China: Rongsheng Heavy Launches VLOC VALE SOHAR Built for OSC]}}. World Maritime News, 9 April 2012. Retrieved 9 April 2012</ref> ''Vale Liwa'' entered service in August 2012, followed by ''Vale Sohar'' in September 2012, ''Vale Saham'' in January 2013, and ''Vale Shinas'' in March 2013. The ships reportedly received additional strengthening due to the ''Vale Beijing'' incident.<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20140726045448/http://www.marine-news-china.com/china-news/shipbuilding/item/517-rongsheng-vlocs-strengthened.html Rongsheng VLOCs strengthened ]}}. Marine News China, 29 April 2012. Retrieved 18 May 2012</ref><ref name="equasis_liwamax" /><ref name="equasis_soharmax" /> The ships built for Oman Shipping Company were later removed from the Det Norske Veritas registry and moved to other [[classification society|classification societies]] such as [[American Bureau of Shipping]] and [[Lloyd's Register]].

The Chinese shipbuilder's ability to deliver any of the very large ore carriers ordered by Vale in time was doubted already before the first ship was built.<ref name="delay_doubts">[http://www.lloydslist.com/ll/sector/dry-cargo/article374281.ece Delivery doubts plague Vale's VLOC newbuilds programme]. Lloyd's List Asia, 30 June 2011. Retrieved 18 November 2011</ref> In May 2011, it was announced that only two or three ''Valemax'' vessels will be delivered from the Chinese shipyard in 2011 instead of the planned six due to delays in construction.<ref name="eship">[http://en.eshiptrading.com/news/d/221/265/ Rongsheng May Deliver Two Large Ore Ships in 2011, Six Fewer Than Planned]. Eshiptrading.com, 26 May 2011. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref><ref name="delivery target">[http://www.aastocks.com/en/news/hk6/0/now.449720.html CH RONGSHENG (01101) 2011 delivery target: 2–3 vessels to VALE COMMON-DRS]. AASTOCKS.com, 24 August 2011. Retrieved 18 November 2011</ref> In the end, only one ship (''Vale China'') was delivered before the end of the year. Furthermore, later reports claimed that the ships ordered by Vale had a capacity of only 380,000 tons even though according to the [[Det Norske Veritas]] database entries all Chinese-built ships have a deadweight tonnage in excess of 400,000 tons and in the past Vale has referred to the ships ordered from Rongsheng as "400,000-ton" vessels. The reduction in cargo capacity, at least on paper, may have been due to the reluctance of Chinese officials to accept the 400,000-ton ships to Chinese ports.<ref name="dnv_orechina" /><ref name="lloyd_diet">[http://www.lloydslist.com/ll/sector/dry-cargo/article385043.ece Vale's giant ore carriers go on a diet]. Lloyd's List, 25 November 2011. Retrieved 29 November 2011</ref><ref name="businesstimes_smaller" />

In April 2012, it was reported that Vale had refused delivery for three ''Valemax'' ships recently completed by Jiangsu Rongsheng Heavy Industries. This was seen as a move against the Chinese officials who have not allowed the 400,000-ton ships to dock in Chinese ports.<ref name="maritimebulletin20042012">[http://www.odin.tc/news/read.asp?articleID=802 Vale refuses delivery on Chinese ships]. Maritime Bulletin, 20 April 2012. Retrieved 21 April 2012</ref> However, the reports were rebutted by RSHI, who called them "inaccurate and unfounded".<ref name="tradewinds_valerefusal">[http://www.tradewindsnews.com/shipsales/666526/rongsheng-scorns-vloc-talk Rongsheng scorns VLOC reports]. Tradewinds. (Registration required)</ref>

==== Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering ====

On 26 October 2009,<ref name="dnv_orebrasil" /> Vale ordered four ''Valemax'' vessels from the South Korean shipbuilder Daewoo Shipbuilding & Marine Engineering (DSME) for $460 million.<ref name="motorship">[http://www.motorship.com/news101/dsme-bags-vloc-order DSME bags VLOC order]. The Motor Ship, 28 October 2009. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref> Further three ships were ordered from DSME in July 2010, bringing the total order to seven 400,000-ton ''Valemax'' vessels.<ref name="maritimepress">[http://eng.maritimepress.com/news/quickViewArticleView.html?idxno=161 DSME wins order 3 VLOCs from Vale]. Maritime Press, 25 June 2010. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref> Despite receiving the order later than the Chinese shipyard, DSME launched the first ''Valemax'' class ore carrier, ''Vale Brasil'', on 31 December 2010 and delivered the ship to Vale in March 2011.<ref name="dnv_orebrasil" />

''Vale Brasil'' was followed by [[MV Vale Rio de Janeiro|''Vale Rio de Janeiro'']] on 22 September 2011,<ref name="dnv_valeriodejaniero" /> [[MS Vale Italia|''Vale Italia'']] on 25 October 2011,<ref name="dnv_oreitalia" /> [[MS Vale Malaysia|''Vale Malaysia'']] on 27 March 2012,<ref name="dnv_valemalaysia" /> [[MS Vale Carajas|''Vale Carajas'']] on 29 May 2012,<ref name="dnv_valecarajas" /> and [[MV Vale Minas Gerais|''Vale Minas Gerais'']] on 13 July 2012.<ref name="dnv_valeminasgerais" /> The last ''Valemax'' ship to be built by DSME, [[MS Ore Korea|''Vale Korea'']], was delivered on 9 April 2013.<ref name="dnv_orekorea" />

==== STX Offshore & Shipbuilding ====

In addition to the ships Vale ordered for itself, more ships of similar size were to be built for other shipping companies and chartered to Vale under exclusive long-term contracts. Eight very large ore carriers were ordered from the South Korean shipbuilder [[STX Offshore & Shipbuilding]] in [[Jinhae]], South Korea (STX Jinhae), and [[Dalian]], China (STX Dalian). The shipping company, [[STX Pan Ocean]], signed a 25-year contract with Vale in 2009.<ref name="man" /><ref name="stx">[http://www.resourceinvestor.com/News/2009/9/Pages/STX-Pan-Ocean-in-pact-with-Vale-to-ship-iron-ore.aspx STX Pan Ocean in pact with Vale to ship iron ore]. Resource Investor, 21 September 2009. Retrieved 4 September 2011</ref> The deadweight tonnage of the ''Valemax'' vessels built by STX, 374,400 tons, is slightly smaller than that of the similar ships built by DSME and RSHI.<ref name="businesstimes_smaller">[http://www.businesstimes.com.sg/sub/shippingtimes/story/0,4574,467131,00.html? Vale iron-ore ship built in Korea is smaller than first planned]. The Business Times, 28 November 2011. Retrieved 29 November 2011</ref><ref name="dnv_valebeijing" />

The first STX-built ''Valemax'' vessel, [[MS Vale Beijing|''Vale Beijing'']], was delivered by [[STX Jinhae]] on 27 September 2011. Although another vessel was expected to take delivery later that year, only one ship was delivered. The second ship, [[MS Sea Qingdao|''Vale Qingdao'']], was delivered also by STX Jinhae on 13 April 2012,<ref name="dnv_seaqingdao" /> but the third and fourth ships, [[MS Sea Espirito Santo|''Vale Espirito Santo'']] and [[MS Vale Indonesia|''Vale Indonesia'']], were built by [[STX Dalian]] and delivered on 17 September 2012 and 30 October 2012, respectively.<ref name="dnv_seaespiritosanto" /><ref name="dnv_seaindonesia" /><ref name="stx_dalian">[http://me.stx.co.kr/pr/groupnews/details/577 Delivering World's Largest VLOC and Best-performing Drillship in A Row]. STX Mobile, 26 July 2012. {{retrieved |access-date=17 September 2012}}</ref> The fifth ship, [[MS Vale Fujiyama|''Vale Fujiyama'']], was again built by STX Jinhae and delivered on 26 November 2012.<ref name="dnv_seafujiyama" /> The sixth ship, [[MS Sea Tubarao|''Vale Tubarao'']], was delivered by STX Dalian on 30 January 2013.<ref name="dnv_seatubarao" /> While both of the two remaining ships were supposed to be delivered by the end of 2013, only [[MS Sea Maranhao|''Vale Maranhao'']] entered service on 29 August.<ref name="stx_valebeijing">[http://eng.maritimepress.com/news/articleView.html?idxno=859 STX acquires world-largest VLOC]. Maritime Press, 28 September 2011. Retrieved 3 October 2011</ref><ref name="dnv_seamaranhao" />

The last ''Valemax'' vessel to be built by STX, originally named ''Vale Ponta da Madeira'' but later referred to by its yard number "STX Dalian 1707", was launched sometime in 2015. However, the vessel was never finished and instead was listed as "for sale" in an unfinished state. In March 2016, it was reported that the last of the original 35 ''Valemax'' vessels to be built had been sold for just $16.8 million.<ref>[http://splash247.com/unfinished-stx-dalian-valemax-sells-for-16-8m/ Unfinished STX Dalian valemax sells for just $16.8m]. Splash 24/7, 10 March 2016. {{retrieved|access-date=15 March 2016}}</ref> Initially anonymous, the buyer was later identified as Pan Ocean (formerly STX Pan Ocean), the shipping company who originally ordered the vessel.<ref>[https://www.lloydslist.com/ll/sector/dry-cargo/article519355.ece Pan Ocean acquires unfinished valemax for $17m]. Lloyd's List, 11 March 2016. {{retrieved|access-date=15 March 2016}}</ref> The unfinished vessel was completed by the Chinese shipyard [[Shanhaiguan Shipbuilding]] and named [[MS Sea Ponta da Madeira|''Sea Ponta da Madeira'']].<ref>[http://splash247.com/shanhaiguan-shipbuilding-to-complete-unfinished-stx-dalian-valemax/ Shanhaiguan Shipbuilding to complete unfinished STX Dalian valemax]. Splash 24/7, 29 April 2016. {{retrieved|access-date=6 May 2016}}</ref>

==== Bohai Shipbuilding Heavy Industry ====

On 30 April 2007 [[Berge Bulk]] signed a contract with the Chinese shipbuilding company [[Bohai Shipbuilding Heavy Industry]] for the construction of four 388,000-ton very large ore carriers. Although initially scheduled for delivery in 2010, the first vessel, [[MS Berge Everest|''Berge Everest'']], was delivered on 23 September 2011.<ref name="dnv_bergeeverest" /> It was followed by [[MS Berge Aconcagua|''Berge Aconcagua'']] on 15 March 2012<ref name="dnv_bergeaconcagua">{{csr|register=DNV|id=28515|shipname=Berge Aconcagua|access-date=7 April 2012}}</ref> and [[MS Berge Jaya|''Berge Jaya'']] on 12 June 2012.<ref name="dnv_bergejaya">{{csr|register=DNV|id=28516|shipname=Berge Jaya|access-date=17 June 2012}}</ref> The remaining ship, [[MS Berge Neblina|''Berge Neblina'']], was initially also scheduled to be delivered in 2012, but entered service on 4 January 2013.<ref name="reuters_berge1st">[https://web.archive.org/web/20160304003223/http://af.reuters.com/article/energyOilNews/idAFL3E7IK0PE20110720 China Bohai Shipbuilding to soon deliver 1st mega dry bulk ship]. Reuters, 20 July 2011. Retrieved 10 December 2011</ref><ref name="dnv_buildingbulk">{{cite web|url=http://www.dnv.no/din_bransje/maritime/publikasjoner/publications/dnvbullkcarrierupdate/2007/3_2007/Buildingtheworldslargestbulkcarriers.asp |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120513033519/http://www.dnv.no/din_bransje/maritime/publikasjoner/publications/dnvbullkcarrierupdate/2007/3_2007/Buildingtheworldslargestbulkcarriers.asp |archive-date=2012-05-13 |title=Building the world's largest bulk carriers|website=Det Norske Veritas|date=30 January 2008|access-date=10 December 2011}}</ref><ref name="dnv_bergeneblina">{{csr|register=DNV|id=28517|shipname=Berge Neblina|access-date=22 January 2013}}</ref>

Had Vale not ordered the ''Valemax'' fleet in 2008, these ships would have become the largest bulk carriers in the world, surpassing Berge Bulk's own [[MS Berge Stahl|''Berge Stahl'']]. The four ships have since been chartered by Vale and, despite slight differences in design and contract date predating that of the ships ordered by Vale, they are also referred to as ''Valemax'' vessels.<ref name="lloyds_berge_valemax">[http://www.lloydslist.com/ll/sector/dry-cargo/article386077.ece http://www.lloydslist.com/ll/sector/dry-cargo/article386077.ece]. Lloyd's List, 8 December 2011. Retrieved 10 December 2011</ref><ref name="reuters_bergeeverest">[https://www.reuters.com/article/shipping-vale-asia-idUSL3E7N81AM20111208?type=companyNews First of Vale's mega ships to arrive in Asia next week]. Reuters, 8 December 2011. Retrieved 8 December 2011</ref>

=== Second series ===

In March 2016, it was reported that three Chinese companies, [[COSCO|China Ocean Shipping (Group) Company (COSCO)]], [[China Merchants Energy Shipping]] and [[Industrial and Commercial Bank of China]] (ICBC), had ordered ten ''Valemax'' vessels each from four Chinese shipyards with a total price of US$2.5 billion.<ref name="vale_30more">[https://www.wsj.com/articles/chinese-shipping-majors-splash-2-5-billion-for-30-giant-valemax-vessels-1457631278 Chinese Shipping Majors Splash $2.5 Billion for 30 Giant Valemax Vessels ]. The Wall Street Journal, 10 March 2016. {{retrieved|access-date=14 March 2016}}</ref> The ''Valemax'' ships ordered by China Merchants Energy Shipping would be built by Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding (4 ships), [[Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding]] (4 ships), and [[China Merchants Group]]-controlled [[China Merchants Heavy Industry|China Merchants Heavy Industry (Jiangsu)]] (2 ships).<ref name="chinaenergy_10ships">[http://www.silkysea.com/2016/03/24/three-chinese-shipbuilders-to-build-ten-vloc-vessels-for-cmes/ Three Chinese Shipbuilders to Build Ten VLOC Vessels for CMES]. Silky Sea, 24 March 2016. {{retrieved|access-date=7 May 2016}}</ref> China COSCO Shipping Corporation awarded the construction of all of its ten 400,000-ton ore carriers to Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding.<ref name="cosco_10ships">{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20160403024408/http://worldmaritimenews.com/archives/187454/coscocs-closes-deal-for-10-vlocs-at-sws/ COSCOCS Closes Deal for 10 VLOCs at SWS]}}. World Maritime News, 1 April 2016. {{retrieved|access-date=7 May 2016}}</ref> ICBC, which would later hand over the vessels to China Marchants Energy Shipping, announced that six of its ships would be built by the Chinese privately owned shipyard [[Yangzijian Shipbuilding]] while the remaining four would be awarded to Qingdao Beihai Shipbuilding.<ref name="icbc">{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20160416020729/http://worldmaritimenews.com/archives/188555/icbc-reveals-builders-of-its-valemax-series/ ICBC Reveals Builders of Its Valemax Series]}}. World Maritime News, 12 April 2016. {{retrieved|access-date=7 May 2016}}</ref><ref>[http://www.newsmaritime.com/2016/chinese-shipping-companies-submit-orders-for-30-valemax-vessels/ Chinese shipping companies submit orders for 30 Valemax vessels]. Maritime News, 7 March 2016. {{retrieved|access-date=7 May 2016}}</ref> The first of the thirty Chinese-built second-generation ''Valemax'' vessels, [[MV Yuan He Hai|''Yuan He Hai'']], was delivered on 11 January 2018<ref name="yuanhehai_dnv" /><ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20180112124738/https://worldmaritimenews.com/archives/240491/sws-hands-over-first-valemax-newbuilding-to-coscocs/ SWS Hands Over First Valemax Newbuilding to COSCOCS]}}. World Maritime News, 12 January 2018. {{retrieved|access-date=19 February 2018}}</ref> and the last one of the series, ''[[Yuan Qian Hai]]'', in January 2020.<ref name="lastvalemax" />

In December 2016, the Japanese shipping company [[NS United]] ordered a single 400,000{{nbsp}}DWT very large ore carrier from [[Japan Marine United]] after signing a 25-year contract with Vale. The vessel, which would become the first ''Valemax'' ship built in Japan, was delivered in December 2019 as ''[[NSU Carajas]]''.<ref name="equasis_nsucarajas" /><ref>[http://fairplay.ihs.com/commerce/article/4279181/ns-united-seals-25-year-charter-deal-with-vale NS United seals 25-year charter deal with Vale]. IHS Fairplay, 12 December 2016. {{retrieved|access-date=9 April 2017}}</ref> A second vessel (''[[NSU Brazil]]''), was ordered in June 2017 and a third (''[[NSU Tubarao]]'') later that year; both were delivered in late 2020.<ref name="japan_thirdvalemax" /><ref name="equasis_nsubrazil" /><ref name="equasis_nsutubarao" />

== Career ==

=== Initial career and ban ===

[[File:Vale Rio de Janeiro 20120108 02.jpg|thumb|400px|[[MV Vale Rio de Janeiro|''Vale Rio de Janeiro'']] arriving at [[Rotterdam]], January 2012.]]

On 24 May 2011, ''Vale Brasil'' received her first cargo at the Brazilian port [[Terminal Marítimo de Ponta da Madeira]], 391,000 tons of iron ore bound for [[Dalian]] in China.<ref name="tex" /> However, the ship turned back towards the [[Atlantic Ocean]] in June after rounding the [[Cape of Good Hope]] and was rerouted to [[Taranto]], [[Italy]].<ref name="reuters">[https://www.reuters.com/article/vale-cargo-idUSN1E75K1UD20110621 Vale reroutes China-bound iron cargo to Italy]. Reuters, 21 June 2011. Retrieved 1 September 2011</ref> There had been speculation that ''Vale Brasil'' was not allowed to enter the Chinese port fully laden, but according to Vale the destination was changed due to commercial, not political reasons.<ref name="leeuniversal">[https://leeuniversal.blogspot.com/2011/06/vale-diverts-china-ore-ship-for.html Vale diverts China ore ship for commercial reasons]. Lee Universal Enterprises, 22 June 2011. Retrieved 1 September 2011</ref> The ship arrived at the port of Taranto on 14 July 2011 to discharge her cargo.<ref name="steelguru">[http://www.steelguru.com/raw_material_news/Vale_Brasil_discharged_iron_ore_carrier_at_Taranto_in_Italy_for_Ilva/216053.html Vale Brasil discharged iron ore carrier at Taranto in Italy for Ilva]. Steelguru, 22 July 2011. Retrieved 1 September 2011</ref> Since then, fully laden ''Valemax'' vessels have unloaded at various ports, such as Dalian in China,<ref name="ban"/> [[SOHAR Port and Freezone|Sohar in Oman]],<ref name="brazilsohar">[http://www.royalhaskoning.co.uk/en-gb/News/Pages/port-of-sohar-iron-ore-jetty.aspx Iron ore mega-ship offloads first 400,000 tonnes at Sohar jetty]. Royal Haskoning, 29 September 2011. Retrieved 4 February 2012</ref> [[Rotterdam]] in the Netherlands,<ref>[http://www.rijnmond.nl/nieuws/08-01-2012/vale-rio-haven-binnengevaren Vale Rio is haven binnengevaren]. Rijnmond, 8 January 2012. {{retrieved|access-date=8 January 2012}}</ref> [[Ōita, Ōita|Ōita]] in [[Japan]],<ref>[https://www.steelorbis.com/steel-news/latest-news/valemax-ore-carrier-docks-in-japan-for-first-time-693547.htm Valemax ore carrier docks in Japan for first time]. SteelOrbis, 19 June 2012. {{retrieved|access-date=24 June 2012}}</ref> [[Dangjin]] in South Korea,<ref>[http://www.vale.com/en/aboutvale/news/pages/porto-sul-coreano-recebe-uma-navio-valemax-pela-primeira-vez.aspx South Korean port receives a Valemax class vessel for the first time]. Vale S.A., 4 October 2013. {{retrieved|access-date=1 November 2013}}</ref> and the transshipment hub Vale has constructed at [[Subic Bay]] in the [[Philippines]].<ref name="reuters_subic" />

On 31 January 2012, the [[Ministry of Commerce of the People's Republic of China]] officially banned dry bulk carriers with capacity exceeding 300,000 tons from entering Chinese ports in order to protect the domestic freight industry. Prior to this, only one of the new very large ore carrier chartered by Vale, ''Berge Everest'', had unloaded Brazilian iron ore at a Chinese port – the ship arrived at Dalian on 28 December 2011 – but this was assumed to be a bureaucratic fluke as no Chinese port has regulatory approval to receive dry bulk carriers of that size.<ref name="ban">[http://www.businesstimes.com.sg/sub/news/story/0,4574,476063,00.html? China bans 400,000 dwt 'Valemax' vessels] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230716173621/https://www.businesstimes.com.sg/sub/news/story/0,4574,476063,00.html |date=16 July 2023 }}. The Business Times, 2 February 2012. Retrieved 4 February 2012</ref>

According to Vale, the discussions about allowing the ''Valemax'' ships to enter Chinese ports were ongoing since the ban came into force<ref>[http://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/News.aspx?ElementId=6fc9cfe2-083b-4eeb-b49d-d902b8debff0 Vale Says Discussions 'Going On' Over China Valemax Access]. Hellenic Shipping News, 23 May 2012. {{retrieved|access-date=23 May 2012}}</ref> and the Chinese officials had given a preliminary go-ahead for the construction of new berths capable of accommodating the 400,000-ton ships.<ref>[http://www.lloydslist.com/ll/sector/ports-and-logistics/article399410.ece China gives preliminary go-ahead to building valemax berths]. Lloyd's List, 29 May 2012. Retrieved 6 June 2012</ref> According to the [[Port of Ningbo|Ningbo Port Company]], the construction of the new port facilities would take two to three years, causing further delays for Vale, which in the meantime was losing $2–3 per ton of ore due to the ban.<ref>[http://www.mineweb.com/mineweb/content/en/mineweb-fast-news?oid=165669&sn=Detail Vale losing $2–$3/t of ore due to China Valemax ban]. Mineweb, 6 December 2012. {{retrieved|access-date=26 July 2013}}</ref><ref>[https://www.forbes.com/sites/greatspeculations/2012/09/04/vales-valemax-service-remains-grounded-in-china/ Vale's Valemax Service Still Faces Hurdles In China]. Forbes, 4 September 2012. Retrieved 7 September 2012</ref> On 15 April 2013, ''Vale Malaysia'' became the first 400,000-ton ''Valemax'' vessel to call a Chinese port. The partially loaded ship docked at the port of [[Lianyungang]] en route from the Vale transshipment hub in Subic Bay, Philippines. However, at the time, the Chinese officials had not yet lifted the ban for fully laden ''Valemax'' vessels.<ref name="valemalaysiainchina">[https://www.scmp.com/business/companies/article/1217335/valemax-enters-china-port-first-time-ban Valemax enters China port for first time since ban]. South China Morning Post, 18 April 2013. {{retrieved |access-date=18 April 2013}}</ref><ref name="valemalaysiainchina2">[http://www.lloydslistdcn.com.au/archive/2013/april/18/chinese-port-first-to-take-in-valemax-giant  Chinese port first to take in valemax giant]. Lloyd's list, 18 April 2013. {{retrieved |access-date=18 April 2013}}</ref> The first fully laden ''Valemax'' vessel to call a Chinese port since 2012, ''Shandong Da Ren'', docked at the Dongjiakou port in Qingdao on 2 October 2014.<ref>[http://www.mineweb.com/mineweb/content/en//mineweb-fast-news?oid=256120&sn=Detail Valemax finally allowed to dock at Chinese port]. MineWeb, 10 October 2014. {{retrieved|access-date=10 October 2014}}</ref> The ban was officially lifted in July 2015.<ref name="ft_ban" /><ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Massot |first=Pascale |title=China's Vulnerability Paradox: How the World's Largest Consumer Transformed Global Commodity Markets |date=2024 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-777140-2 |location=New York, NY, United States of America |pages=128-129}}</ref>

=== Sale of ships ===

Originally, Vale planned to own and manage a fleet of 19 ''Valemax'' vessels by itself in order to control the wildly fluctuating charter prices for large bulk carriers which had dropped from US$233,988 per day in June 2008 to as low as US$2,400 by December of the same year. However, because of the [[Great Recession]] and Chinese ports' reluctance to accept the fully laden ships, the new board of directors decided to focus capital allocation on mining. As a result, Vale decided to sell the ships and charter them back under long-term contracts.<ref name="steelguru20111222">[http://www.steelguru.com/raw_material_news/Vale_looking_to_sell_Valemax_iron_ore_carriers_Report/242353.html Vale looking to sell Valemax iron ore carriers]. Steel Guru, 22 December 2011. Retrieved 22 December 2011</ref> Although Vale was expected to suffer financial losses from selling the ships, they would have been covered by the profit from iron ore sales even at depressed ore prices if only one or two full shipments could be unloaded in Chinese ports.<ref name="tradewinds20111222">[http://www.tradewindsnews.com/drycargo/661582/vale-vlocs-a-lossleader Vale VLOCs a "loss-leader"]. TradeWinds, 22 December 2011. Retrieved 23 December 2011</ref>

In September 2014, Vale signed a framework agreement with the state-owned [[COSCO|China Ocean Shipping (Group) Company (COSCO)]], establishing a strategic cooperation in iron ore shipping.<ref>[http://saladeimprensa.vale.com/en/releases/interna.asp?id=22775 Vale and Cosco sign cooperation agreement on VLOCs]. 11 September 2014. {{retrieved|access-date=1 October 2014}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> Later that month, a 25-year freight contract was signed between Vale and China Merchants Group. As part of the agreement, the Chinese shipping company will construct 10 new very large ore carriers to transport iron ore from Brazil to China.<ref>[http://saladeimprensa.vale.com/en/releases/interna.asp?id=22781 Vale and China Merchants Group sign agreement on VLOCs]. Vale SA, 26 September 2014. {{retrieved|access-date=1 October 2014}}</ref> Following these agreements, China's ban on ''Valemax'' vessels has been effectively lifted, allowing fully laden ships to enter Chinese ports.<ref>[http://www.mining.com/valemax-ban-effectively-lifted-80770/ Valemax ban 'effectively' lifted]. Mining.com, 24 September 2014. {{retrieved|access-date=1 October 2014}}</ref>

In May 2015, four ships were sold to [[China Ore Shipping|China Ore Shipping Pte. Ltd]]., a joint venture between COSCO and [[China Shipping Development Company]], for US$445 million.<ref name="chinaoreshipping">[http://en.cosco.com/art/2015/5/20/art_773_70260.html COSCO and China Shipping Signed Vessel Purchase Agreement with Vale]. COSCO. {{retrieved|access-date=24 June 2015}}</ref> These were the first ''Valemax'' vessels to officially change ownership. Later, four more ships were sold to [[China Merchants Energy Shipping]].<ref name="cmes_sale" /> In December 2015, Vale announced that the remaining 11 ''Valemax'' ships owned by the mining company would be sold and leased back from the new owners.<ref>[https://www.reuters.com/article/brazil-vale-sa-idUSL1N13T1B720151204 UPDATE 1-Vale says Valemax ship sale, leaseback could fetch $1.1 bln]. Reuters, 4 December 2015. {{retrieved|access-date=5 December 2015}}</ref> The last ''Valemax'' vessels were reportedly sold in December 2017.<ref>{{usurped|1=[https://web.archive.org/web/20171211081546/https://worldmaritimenews.com/archives/237526/vale-sells-final-valemax-bulkers-to-bocomm/ Vale Sells Final Valemax Bulkers to Bocomm]}}. World Maritime News, 11 December 2017. {{retrieved|access-date=28 December 2017}}</ref>

=== Incidents ===

==== Structural failure of ''Vale Beijing'' ====
On 5 December 2011, it was reported that ''Vale Beijing'', operated by STX Pan Ocean, had suffered structural damage during her first cargo loading and was in danger of sinking at the port of Ponta da Madeira in Brazil due to seawater entering ruptured ballast tanks and cargo holds. The South Korean-built ''Valemax'' ship, partially loaded with 260,000 tons of iron ore,<ref name="amountofcargo">[http://www.ubs.wallst.com/ubs/mkt_story.asp?docKey=1329-N1E7B60F8-1&first=0 Vale says put 260,000 tonnes of ore on damaged ship]. Wall Street on Demand, 25 December 2011. {{retrieved |access-date=25 December 2011}}</ref> was towed away from Pier 1 by tugboats in the following day, and as a precaution against environmental damage, the Brazilian authorities requested her fuel tanks to be emptied.<ref name="mb_vb_fuel">[http://www.odin.tc/news/read.asp?articleID=280 Vale Beijing Update]. Maritime Bulletin, 9 December 2011. Retrieved 11 December 2011</ref> Because there are no facilities to unload iron ore from the ship at Ponta da Madeira and no large shipyards in the region, emergency repairs had to be performed by divers and the cargo redistributed while the ship was anchored offshore before it could be towed to a shipyard.<ref name="reuters_valebeijing">[https://web.archive.org/web/20160304073237/http://af.reuters.com/article/commoditiesNews/idAFL3E7N60CK20111206 Huge Vale ore carrier disabled at Brazil port]. Reuters, 6 December 2011. Retrieved 6 December 2011</ref><ref name="valebeijing_miningweekly">[http://www.miningweekly.com/article/huge-vale-ore-carrier-may-sink-at-brazil-port-2011-12-06 Huge Vale ore carrier may sink at Brazil port]. Mining Weekly, 6 December 2011. Retrieved 6 December 2011</ref><ref name="reuters712">[https://www.reuters.com/article/us-vale-shipping-idUSTRE7B512120111206 Vale port moves damaged ore ship from berth]. Reuters, 6 December 2011. Retrieved 6 December 2011</ref>

The cause of the damage has not been published by STX, but design or construction flaws, material fatigue, and incorrect loading have all been suspected.<ref name="mb_vb_fuel" /><ref name="seanews_valebeijing">[http://www.seanews.com.tr/article/ACCIDENTS/73071/Vale-Beijing/ VALE BEIJING: Situation remains serious] SeaNews Turkey, 8 December 2011. Retrieved 11 December 2011</ref> According to calculations performed by DNV, the damage was not caused by global strength issues or single pass loading, but is assumed to be related to local buckling strength in some areas of the web frames in the aft ballast tanks.<ref name="dnv2012">[http://www.dnv.com/press_area/press_releases/2012/valebeijingincidentnotrelatedtoglobalstrengthissuesorsinglepassloading.asp Vale Beijing incident not related to global strength issues or single pass loading]. Det Norske Veritas, 16 January 2012. Retrieved 22 January 2012</ref> ''Vale Beijing'' remained anchored off Ponta da Madeira with a crawler crane on the deck and an oceangoing tug standing by<ref>[http://www.odin.tc/news/read.asp?articleID=484 VLOC Vale Beijing still anchored off Sao Luis, offloading ore in barges]. Maritime Bulletin, 20 January 2012. Retrieved 4 February 2012</ref> until 19 February 2012, when it left [[São Luís, Maranhão|São Luís]] for Oman. After unloading at Sohar, the ship headed to South Korea for dry docking and arrived at STX shipyard in Jinhae, where it was delivered in September 2011, for inspection and repairs on 21 April 2012.<ref name="valebeijingdrydocking">{{cite web|url=http://www.businessweek.com/news/2012-04-04/vale-beijing-heading-to-south-korea-for-inspections-owner-says|title=Vale Beijing Heading to South Korea for Inspections, Owner Says|website=Bloomberg Businessweek|date=4 April 2012|access-date=7 April 2012}}{{dead link|date=August 2026}}</ref> ''Vale Beijing'' returned to service in July 2012.<ref>[http://www.miningweekly.com/article/vales-huge-iron-ore-ship-back-in-service-after-maiden-accident-2012-07-16 Vale's huge iron-ore ship back in service after maiden accident]. Mining Weekly, 16 July 2012. Retrieved 16 July 2012</ref>

Had ''Vale Beijing'' sunk at the pier instead of being moved to an anchorage area outside the port shortly after the leak was detected, the incident would have severely delayed the operations at the port, which ships out about 10 percent of the world's iron ore production.<ref name="reuters_valebeijing" /> On 11 November 1994, while ''Vale Beijing'' delayed the loading of only 750,000 tons of iron ore,<ref name="reuters_delay">[http://uk.reuters.com/article/vale-brazil-shipping-idUKN1E7B50BS20111206 Damaged Vale ore ship moved, shipments normalized]{{dead link|date=September 2024|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}. Reuters, 6 December 2011. Retrieved 9 November 2011</ref> ''Trade Daring'', a 145,000 DWT [[ore-bulk-oil carrier]], broke in two at the same location due to incorrect loading, blocking the deepwater pier of Ponta da Madeira for more than six weeks before the wreck was removed and [[scuttling|scuttled]] offshore.<ref name="costofsubstandard">[http://www.rbna.org.br/english/tradedaring.htm Trade Daring]. The Brazilian Register of Shipping (RBNA). Retrieved 7 December 2011</ref>

After the incident, the China Shipowners' Association (CSA) questioned the safety of the 400,000-ton ore carriers commissioned by Vale. CSA was particularly concerned about the ability of the newly built ships to withstand various sea conditions and the pollution resulting from fuel oil leaks in case of structural damage<ref name="chinaquestions">[https://en.mercopress.com/2011/12/14/china-questions-safety-of-brazil-s-dry-bulk-carriers-the-world-s-largest China questions safety of Brazil's dry bulk carriers, the world's largest]. MercoPress, 14 December 2011. Retrieved 23 December 2011</ref> — each ''Valemax'' ship can carry around 10,000 tons of fuel oil.<ref name="mainpart" /> In January 2012, China officially banned the vessels from Chinese ports.<ref name="ban" /> However, in April 2013, the China Shipping Association confirmed that the first Valemax vessel was allowed to dock in the Chinese [[Lianyungang Port|port of Lianyungang]] in [[Jiangsu]] province.<ref>China permits giant Valemax to dock, ''Hook. Leslie, [https://www.ft.com/content/ab14aba8-a7fb-11e2-b031-00144feabdc0 Financial Times – Shipping (18 April, 2013)] ''</ref> The ban was officially lifted in July 2015 as China's transport ministry and [[National Development and Reform Commission]] announced that four ports would be opened up for 400,000-ton vessels.<ref name="ft_ban">[https://www.ft.com/content/10a4f69e-213f-11e5-ab0f-6bb9974f25d0 China lifts ban on giant Valemax ships]. ''Financial Times'', 3 July 2015. {{retrieved|access-date=4 July 2015}}</ref>

==== Grounding of ''Vale Indonesia'' ====

On 7 September 2013, ''Vale Indonesia'' ran aground on a sandbar about {{convert|40|nmi}} north of [[São Luís, Maranhão|São Luís]]. The vessel, operated by STX Pan Ocean, was fully laden with 390,000 tons of iron ore bound for Vale's transhipment hub in Subic Bay. Two ballast tanks were reportedly breached, but there were no injuries or pollution, and the vessel was not in danger of sinking.<ref>[http://news.odin.tc/index.php?page=view/article/822/Valemax-Vale-Indonesia-grounded-and-breached-off-Ponta-da-Madeira-Brazil Valemax Vale Indonesia grounded and breached off Ponta da Madeira, Brazil]. Maritime Bulletin, 9 September 2013. {{retrieved|access-date=11 September 2013}}</ref><ref>[http://www.seatrade-global.com/news/americas/valemax-vale-indonesia-hits-sandbar-in-brazil-port.html  Valemax Vale Indonesia hits sandbar in Brazil port]. Seatrade Global, 10 September 2013. {{retrieved|access-date=11 September 2013}}</ref>

==== Allision of ''NSU Carajas'' ====

On 28 November 2020, arriving at [[Ponta da Madeira]] terminal in Brazil, ''NSU Carajas'' [[Admiralty_law#Allision|allided]] with two Liberian-flagged {{DWT|179000}} bulk carriers, ''Star Janni'' and ''Korona D'', already berthed there. While there were no injuries among the crews or the terminal personnel, the ships suffered structural damage and were subsequently moved to an anchorage area outside of the port for inspection.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nsuship.co.jp/uploads/2020/12/NSU-CARAJAS-Collision-at-Brazil.pdf|title=Ore Carrier NSU CARAJAS Collision with Other Vessels at Brazil|publisher=NS United|date=28 November 2020|access-date=13 December 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.maritime-executive.com/article/three-vessels-make-contact-in-accident-at-brazilian-terminal|title=Three Vessels Make Contact in Accident at Brazilian Terminal  |publisher=Maritime Executive|date=30 November 2020|access-date=13 December 2020}}</ref>

== Naming ==

All ''Valemax'' vessels, with the exception of those owned and operated by Berge Bulk, were initially given names consisting of the word ''Vale'' and a place name, either one related to the mining operations of Vale S.A. in Brazil or a potential destination for the new iron ore carriers. However, none of the original 35 ''Valemax'' vessels retains its original name.

When Vale signed a $500 million contract with the Chinese shipping company Shandong Shipping for the operation of four ''Valemax'' vessels, the ships were given new names beginning with ''Shandong''.<ref>[http://uk.finance.yahoo.com/news/shandong-shipping-agrees-operate-vales-115058749.html Shandong Shipping agrees to operate Vale's giant iron ore ships]. Yahoo! Finance, 1 November 2013. {{retrieved|access-date=1 November 2013}}</ref> Similarly, when four ''Valemax'' vessels were sold to China Ore Shipping, the vessels were given names beginning with ''Yuan'' and ending with ''Hai''.<ref name="chinaoreshipping" /> Four more ''Valemax'' vessels were given names starting with ''Pacific'' after Vale sold the ships to [[China Merchants Energy Shipping]].<ref name="cmes_sale">[https://www.vesselfinder.com/news/4353-China-Merchants-Energy-Shipping-Signed-COA-with-VALE China Merchants Energy Shipping Signed COA with VALE]. Vesselfinder.com, 29 September 2015. {{retrieved|access-date=13 October 2015}}</ref>

Additionally, numerous ''Valemax'' vessels have been renamed by replacing ''Vale'' with ''Ore'' or ''Sea'' but retaining the second part of the name. ''Vale Sohar'', ''Vale Saham'', ''Vale Liwa'' and ''Vale Shinas'' have also been renamed ''Sohar Max'', ''Saham Max'', ''Liwa Max'' and ''Shinas Max'', respectively.

== Design ==

[[File:Vale Sohar in Nantong.jpg|thumb|left|400px|''Vale Sohar'', built by Jiangsu Rongsheng Heavy Industries (RSHI), awaiting delivery to Oman Shipping Company in [[Nantong]], [[China]], in September 2012. Note the minor differences from the South Korean-built [[MV Vale Rio de Janeiro|''Vale Rio de Janeiro'']].]]

=== General characteristics ===

Although similar in size, there are some differences in main dimensions, cargo capacity, machinery and external appearance between the ''Valemax'' ships built in South Korea, China and Japan. While the first series of 35 ships was more diverse, all 30 Chinese-built ''Valemax'' vessels of the second series are based on the same standard design, ''SDARI 400OC'', by [[Shanghai Merchant Ship Design & Research Institute]] (SDARI).<ref name="seaweb">{{csr|register=SEAWEB|id=9807724|shipname=QINGDAO BEIHAI OC400K-1|access-date=9 November 2016}}</ref> The three Japanese-built vessels, however, represent another standard design, ''G400OC''.<ref name="seaweb_nsucarajas" />

''Valemax'' ships are {{convert|360|to|362|m|ft|0}} long,<ref name="dnv1" /><ref name="dnv2">[http://www.dnv.in/industry/maritime/publicationsanddownloads/publications/dnvbullkcarrierupdate/2008/4_2008/theworldslargest.asp The world's largest ore carriers]. Det Norske Veritas. Retrieved 1 September 2011</ref> making them some of the longest ships currently in service. With a maximum [[Draft (hull)|draught]] of between {{convert|22|and|23|m|ft|0}} while loaded, the ships are limited only to a few deepwater ports in Brazil, Europe and China.<ref name="miningweekly2">[http://www.miningweekly.com/print-version/vale-plans-iron-ore-production-rise-of-63-by-2015-and-fleet-of-giant-ships-to-supply-china-2011-04-22 Vale mulling 63% iron-ore production increase by 2015 ]. Mining Weekly, 22 April 2011. Retrieved 2 September 2011</ref><ref name="machinesupport">[https://www.machinesupport.com/english/news-6.html Machine Support services on world's largest dry bulk carrier]. Machine Support News. Retrieved 2 September 2011</ref> In ballast, the ships draw around {{convert|12|m|ft}} of water.<ref name="brazilsohar" /> The breadth of the ''Valemax'' ships is about {{convert|65|m|ft|0}}.<ref name="dnv1" /><ref name="dnv_valebeijing" /><ref name="seaweb_nsucarajas" /><ref name="dnv2" /> The size of the ships is limited mainly by Chinese ports, and the ships of this size are generally referred to as [[Chinamax]] vessels.

The largest bulk carriers ever built, the ''Valemax'' vessels have seven [[cargo hold]]s with a total gross volume of almost {{convert|220000|m3|cuyd|0|sigfig=2}}.<ref name="mainpart">[https://www.scribd.com/doc/58589958/Mv-Vale-Brasil-Ship-s-Particulars M.V. Vale Brasil – Ships particulars]. Retrieved 26 August 2011</ref> In addition to increasing the strength of the hull, special attention has also been paid to improving the speed and efficiency of the loading and discharging operations. Each cargo hold can be fully loaded by a [[shiploader]] in a single step with a loading rate of 13,500 tonnes per hour and can carry almost as much iron ore as a small [[Panamax]] carrier. In addition, the space inside the cargo hold that cannot be reached by [[Grab (tool)|grabs]] during discharging, the so-called "dead spots", is minimized.<ref name="dnv2" /> With a deadweight tonnage of about 400,000 tons, a fully laden ''Valemax'' vessel is carrying as much iron ore as around 11,150 trucks, enough to produce steel for three [[Golden Gate]] bridges.<ref name="tex">[http://www.texreport.co.jp/xenglish/eng-genryou/201105/201105261004Thu-2.html Vale Brasil Sails For The Port Of Dalian In China] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304032711/http://www.texreport.co.jp/xenglish/eng-genryou/201105/201105261004Thu-2.html |date=4 March 2016 }}. The TEX Report, 31 May 2011. Retrieved 1 September 2011</ref><ref name="valeship">[http://75.125.136.98/~appvale/english.html Interactive presentation] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110529215122/http://75.125.136.98/~appvale/english.html |date=29 May 2011 }}. Vale S.A. Retrieved 28 August 2011</ref> The first 35 ''Valemax'' ships were said to be capable of carrying about 15% of the annual iron ore exports from Brazil to all destinations if each ship does four round trips per year.<ref name="cp20130717">[http://www.carbonpositive.net/media-centre/industry-updates/1448-the-chinamax-aka-valemax-an-iron-ore-carrier-drama.html  The 'Chinamax' aka* 'Valemax': an (iron) ore carrier drama]. Carbon Positive, 17 July 2013. {{retrieved|access-date=26 July 2013}}</ref>

Like most modern bulk carriers, ''Valemax'' vessels are powered by a single two-stroke low-speed [[crosshead]] [[Two-stroke diesel engine|diesel engine]] directly coupled to a fixed-pitch [[propeller]]. The ships built by DSME and STX in South Korea are powered by [[straight-seven engine|7-cylinder]] [[MAN Diesel|MAN B&W]] 7S80ME-C8 and 7S80ME-C engines, respectively, and the ships built by RSHI and Bohai Shipbuilding Heavy Industry have [[Wärtsilä]] 7RT-flex82T and 7RT-flex84T engines, respectively.<ref name="man">[http://www.mandieselturbo.de/1014546/Presse/Pressemeldungen/Fachpressemeldungen/Marine-Power/Low-Speed/ME-Engine-Firmly-Established-in-Brazilian-Market.html ME-Engine Firmly Established in Brazilian Market]. MAN Diesel & Turbo. Retrieved 1 September 2011</ref> Both MAN and Wärtsilä engines will have a [[maximum continuous rating]] of around {{convert|29000|kW|hp|abbr=on}} when turning the {{convert|10|m|ft|0|adj=on}} propeller at 76–78 rpm, giving the ships a service speed of around {{convert|15|kn}} while burning almost 100 tons of [[heavy fuel oil]] per day.<ref name="dnv_orekorea" /><ref name="dnv2" /><ref name="valeslides">[http://www.slideshare.net/SistemaFIEB/vale-a-global-strategic-partner Vale – A Global Strategic Partner]. Vale S.A. Retrieved 1 September 2011</ref><ref name="lloyds_risks">[http://www.lloydslist.com/ll/sector/dry-cargo/article341546.ece Vale's fleet ambitions loaded with super-sized risks]. Lloyd's List, 30 July 2010. Retrieved 4 September 2011</ref> However, because of the vessels' large size, emissions per [[Units of transportation measurement|cargo ton-mile]] are very low; thus the ''Valemax'' vessels are in fact among the most efficient long-distance dry bulk carriers in service – Vale has reported a 35% drop in emissions per ton of cargo carried in comparison to older ships.<ref name="man2">[http://www.mandieselturbo.net/files/news/filesof15529/DF_2011-2.pdf World's Largest Bulk Carrier Uses Low-Speed B&W Power on Chinese Route] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120331070755/http://www.mandieselturbo.net/files/news/filesof15529/DF_2011-2.pdf |date=31 March 2012 }}. Diesel Facts 2/2011, page 9. MAN Diesel, 2011. Retrieved 26 August 2011</ref> In the second series, the main engine has been changed to a more efficient MAN B&W 7G80ME-C9 engine producing about {{convert|33000|kW|hp|abbr=on}} at 72 rpm,<ref name="seaweb" /> while claiming a further 15% to 20% reduction in carbon dioxide emissions.<ref>[https://www.vesselfinder.com/news/11657-Green-vessel-built-on-a-Vale-initiative-loads-for-the-first-time-at-the-Tubaro-port "Green" vessel built on a Vale initiative loads for the first time at the Tubarão port]. Vessel Finder, 28 February 2018. {{retrieved|access-date=28 February 2018}}</ref> The Japanese-built ships have 7RT-flex82T engines rated at {{convert|24600|kW|hp|abbr=on}} and 74 rpm, slightly less than their South Korean- or Chinese-built equivalents.<ref name="seaweb_nsucarajas" />

=== Size record ===

[[File:Bateaux comparaison2 with Allure.svg|thumb|400px|''Vale Brasil'' compared to other recent record-holder ships.]]

The new ships are considerably larger than the previous record holder, 364,767-ton [[MS Berge Stahl|''Berge Stahl'']], which had been the largest bulk carrier in the world since it was built in 1986. While the draft of the old vessel is the same as that of the ''Valemax'' vessels — {{convert|23|m|ft|0}} — the new ships are {{convert|20|m|ft|0}} longer and {{convert|1.5|m|ft|1}} wider than the old freighter, and can carry about 10% more cargo.<ref name="dnv_bergestahl">{{csr|register=DNV|id=14702|shipname=Berge Stahl|access-date=18 April 2013}}</ref>

The ''Valemax'' vessels are also the second largest ships in service by deadweight tonnage, second only to the [[TI-class supertanker]]s that have a deadweight tonnage of over 440,000 tons.<ref name="ti">{{cite web |url=http://www.tankersinternational.com/fleet_list.php?type=1&order=year_down |title=Fleet List |author=Tankers International |year=2008 |work=tankersinternational.com |publisher=Tankers International |access-date=7 July 2010 |archive-date=3 September 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100903142826/http://www.tankersinternational.com/fleet_list.php?type=1&order=year_down }}</ref> They are still far from the largest ship ever constructed — ''[[Seawise Giant]]'' (labeled as the ''Knock Nevis'' in the adjacent image), built in 1979 and broken up in 2009, was {{convert|458.46|m|ft}} long and had a deadweight tonnage of 564,650 tons<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.aukevisser.nl/supertankers/id23.htm |title=Jahre Viking | author=Auke Visser | work=International Super Tankers | access-date=24 August 2011}}</ref> — and also considerably longer than the longest ship currently in service, the {{convert|400|m|ft|0|adj=on}} [[container ship]] ''[[Barzan (ship)|Barzan]]''.<ref>{{csr|register=DNV|id=33829|shipname=Barzan|access-date=27 June 2015}}</ref>

== Criticism ==
Vale's decision to construct a fleet of 400,000-ton ore carriers was widely criticized by other shipping companies. The new ''Valemax'' ships, expected to cut the company's transportation costs by 20–25%,<ref name="25-25">[https://web.archive.org/web/20160305080407/http://uk.reuters.com/article/idUKLDE75G1QN20110617 Vale mega ships to cut freight costs by 20–25 pct]. Reuters, 17 June 2011. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref> were blamed for driving down the freight rates for the entire industry, swelling the already oversupplied bulk transportation market and stalling the recovery of the shipping business after the [[Great Recession]]. The freight rates, down 80% from 2008, were expected to drop further down to the levels of 1977.<ref name="drop1977">[https://safewaters.wordpress.com/2010/10/22/shipping-vales-giant-ships-to-drive-rates-to-1977-lows/ Vale's giant ships 'to drive rates to 1977 lows']. Lloyd's List, 22 October 2010. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref> According to the chief executive of the [[Baltic and International Maritime Council]], ''Valemax'' vessels could displace up to 168 150,000–180,000-ton [[capesize]] bulk carriers, around 15% of the existing fleet, from the long-haul voyages and force them to less profitable shorter routes.<ref name="comnow">[http://www.commodities-now.com/reports/general/4422-mega-ships-to-stall-maritime-recovery.html Mega-Ships to stall maritime recovery]. Commodities Now, December 2010. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref><ref name="businessweek">[https://web.archive.org/web/20110502045045/http://www.businessweek.com/news/2011-04-27/vale-brasil-sends-shipping-returns-plummeting-freight-markets.html Vale Brasil Sends Shipping Returns Plummeting: Freight Markets]. Business Week, 27 April 2011. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref> Vale responded to the criticism by stating that the company aims to permanently cut the costs of Atlantic-Pacific dry bulk shipping to make Brazilian ore more competitive against iron ore produced in Australia, which is closer to major customers in Asia.<ref name="drop1977" /><ref name="steelhome2">[https://en.steelhome.cn/2011/07/06/n506002.html Vale New Giant Ships to be Built in China and Korea]. SteelHome, 6 July 2011. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref>

Vale also faced opposition from the China Shipowners' Association, which claimed that the Brazilian mining company is seeking to control the freight market as it has already done with the iron ore prices. In the past, the Chinese ports were not allowed to increase their capacity to more than 300,000 tons for dry bulk carriers due to safety and environmental concerns. If the 400,000-ton ''Valemax'' vessels are allowed to Chinese ports, Vale's monopoly on the route may result in losses for other shipping companies operating capesize ore carriers.<ref name="steelhome">[https://newsen.steelhome.cn/2011/07/26/n513736.html China's Shippers Lobby to Foil Vale's Ore Fleet]. SteelHome, 28 July 2011. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref> When ''Vale Brasil'' was diverted to Italy on her maiden voyage, there was speculation that the domestic steel industry of China had urged the authorities to protect their commercial interests.<ref name="steelhome2"/> However, Vale has also received support from the Chinese steel companies as they would benefit from lower transportation costs.<ref>[http://www.trefis.com/stock/vale/articles/112838/love-for-china-weigh-on-vale/2012-05-10 Vale's Giant Ships Get Support from Chinese Steelmakers]. Trefix, 10 May 2012. Retrieved 7 September 2012</ref>

As a precaution against a prolonged ban on ''Valemax'' vessels from the Chinese ports, Vale started constructing both land- and offshore-based [[transshipment]] hubs where iron ore can be loaded to smaller ships for final delivery. ''Ore Fabrica'', a 280,000 DWT crude oil tanker converted in China, arrived at [[Subic Bay]], [[Philippines]], in late January 2012.<ref name="reuters_subic">[https://www.reuters.com/article/vale-philippines-idUSL4E8CV24M20120131 Vale readies iron ore transshipment hub in Philippines]. Reuters, 31 January 2012. Retrieved 4 February 2012</ref> A second transshipment vessel, ''Ore Sossego'', entered service in 2013.<ref name="ihs_transhipment_scrap">[https://fairplay.ihs.com/commerce/article/4295656/vale-ends-transhipment-as-floating-station-sold-for-scrap Vale ends transhipment as floating station sold for scrap]. IHS Fairplay, 27 December 2017. {{retrieved|access-date=28 December 2017}}</ref> This backup plan was criticized by the vice-executive chairman of the CSA, [[Zhang Shouguo]], who called it "waste of resource" and questioned Vale's ability to run the fleet as properly as professional shipping companies.<ref name="transshipmenthubs">[http://www.lloydslist.com/ll/sector/dry-cargo/article385524.ece Gloves come off in China's Vale scrap]. Lloyd's List, 1 December 2011. {{retrieved |access-date=23 December 2011}}</ref><ref name="zhang_interview">[http://eng.csoa.cn/Reports/201112/t20111206_1162695.html China Shipowners' Association's Comment and View on Vale's Construction of Transshipment Hub and Distribution Centre in Philippines and Malaysia to Transport Iron Ore Imported by China]. China Shipowners' Association, 6 December 2011. {{retrieved|access-date=23 December 2011}}</ref> The transshipment operations ended in 2017, and both ''Ore Fabrica'' and ''Ore Sossego'' were [[shipbreaking|sold for scrap]].<ref name="ihs_transhipment_scrap" />

In May 2012, the largest Chinese operator of dry bulk carriers, state-owned China Ocean Shipping (Group) Company (COSCO), claimed that Vale had refused to use the company's ships since March as a protest against banning the ''Valemax'' vessels from Chinese ports. Vale has refused to give comments on the issue.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.businessweek.com/news/2012-05-08/cosco-says-vale-shuns-its-vessels-on-china-mega-ship-ban|title=Cosco Says Vale Shuns Its Vessels on China Mega-Ship Ban|website=Bloomberg Businessweek|date=9 May 2012|access-date=18 May 2012}}{{dead link|date=August 2026}}</ref>

[[Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva]], the former president of Brazil, also publicly criticized Vale's former CEO [[Roger Agnelli]] for the decision to purchase ships from Asian shipyards instead of building them in Brazil, especially since da Silva has been trying to revitalize the country's shipbuilding industry to foster job growth and increase local demand for steel and other products. Agnelli, who later left his position following continued criticism, replied that the Brazilian shipyards lacked the capacity to build such ships and stated that during the past few years Vale had commissioned 51 vessels from Brazilian shipyards.<ref name="bulkinside">[http://www.bulkinside.com/node/2553 Brazil Vale takes delivery of 400,000-ton ore carrier]. Bulk Inside, 19 May 2011. Retrieved 5 September 2011</ref>
